tagline.text: A hidden Bontoc village where sea clouds drift over stone-walled terraces

items.credit: Tyrel Fang-asan Faniswa / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons
Tyrel Fang-asan Faniswa / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A mountain village just 30-odd minutes up from Bontoc town by jeepney, where rice terraces built from stacked stone fill a valley in tiers. Climbing Mount Kupapey before dawn to look down on the terraces beneath a sea of clouds is the highlight of a visit here.

Maligcong is a highland barangay under Bontoc, the capital of Mountain Province. Seven small hamlets — including Pabarey and Pangorao — are scattered across the mountainside northeast of Bontoc town, with rice terraces stepping down the valley between them. Unlike the already well-known Banaue and Batad, Maligcong has only recently become known to travelers, so it still feels more like a place people live than a tourist site.

The defining feature of these terraces is that the paddy walls are built from stone rather than earth. Bontoc people have stacked stone gathered from the mountains, piece by piece, into tall retaining walls, then flooded the terraces above them to grow rice. When the sun catches them, the gray stone lines stand out sharply against the green paddies, creating a geometric look quite different from the earth-walled terraces of Ifugao. Villagers still plant and harvest by hand, on paddies passed down through generations.
The village's history hasn't been easy. Oral tradition says the ancestors moved several times before settling here, and near the end of World War II, in
, Japanese troops burned the village, leaving only one house standing. The road that cars use today wasn't built until
, and electricity didn't arrive until
. Even now, the whole village settles into quiet early each night.

Maligcong's appeal lies less in flashy sights than in the slow rhythm of a pre-dawn climb, a walk along the paddy walls, and time spent at a homestay. It suits travelers who want to see rice terraces without the crowds, and anyone who enjoys light hiking and photography, and it fits well into a Cordillera loop combined with Sagada and Banaue.

blocks.title: Sunrise and sea of clouds from Mount Kupapey

children.text: Mount Kupapey (also called Kofapey), at about
elevation, is the centerpiece of a Maligcong trip. Set out around
and climb for
1–2 hours
, and the sun rises through the pines with the terraces and a sea of clouds spread out below.

On the way down from Kupapey, a popular route follows the top of the stone paddy walls all the way into the village. Walking along the narrow stonework, you pass right by the rice, the water channels, and villagers at work in the fields.

blocks.title: The view from the other side, at Mount Fato

children.text: Mount Fato (also called Parutan locally), at about
elevation, looks down over the whole terrace system from the opposite side of Kupapey. Its rockier terrain gives the view a rougher, more bracing feel.

blocks.title: Terrace views from the village viewpoint

children.text: If a hike feels like too much, the viewpoint along the road near the jeepney terminus offers a satisfying look at the tiered paddies too. The stonework's texture stands out best when the afternoon sun slants across it.

blocks.title: A mountain night at a homestay

children.text: Staying at a simple homestay run by a village family, eating a home-cooked meal, and watching a sky full of stars are among Maligcong's real pleasures. Temperatures drop noticeably at night, making it a good match for a bonfire and a cup of coffee.

The Bontoc Museum in Bontoc town is a small museum introducing the tools, old photographs, and traditional houses of Cordillera peoples. Stopping in before or after your Maligcong trip helps put the village's culture in context.

items.title: Day 1
items.subtitle: Arrival in Bontoc and a village walk

children.text: Arrive in Bontoc on the overnight bus from Manila, breakfast at a restaurant in town
Visit the Bontoc Museum (check opening hours), shop and get cash
Board a Maligcong-bound jeepney from the stop behind the public market
Check in to your homestay, pay the environmental registration fee, book a guide
Roadside viewpoint and a walk along the paddy walls, explore the village
Dinner at the homestay, early to bed
Set out up Mount Kupapey with your guide, headlamps on
Take in the sunrise, sea of clouds, and terrace views from the summit
Descend along the paddy walls back toward the village
Breakfast at the homestay, then pack up
Return to Bontoc by jeepney or chartered vehicle, continue toward Sagada or Banaue

If you have extra time, a 3-day, 2-night plan that adds a climb up Mount Fato on the afternoon of the second day, with one more night, is also worthwhile. Jeepney schedules change often, so check with your homestay host the day before.
Coda Lines runs a daily overnight bus to Bontoc from the HM terminal in Cubao, Manila. It takes about
10–12 hours
, with fares of around
depending on seat class. Seats are limited, so book ahead for weekends and holidays.
Take a bus from Manila to Baguio, about
4–6 hours
, then catch a Bontoc- or Sagada-bound bus (GL Trans and others) near the Dangwa terminal in Baguio. The mountain drive along Halsema Highway takes about
5–6 hours
, for a fare of around
. The road has many curves, so bring motion-sickness medicine.
Jeepneys to Maligcong leave a few times a day (usually around 8 AM, noon, 2 PM, and 4 PM) from the stop behind Bontoc's public market. The ride takes about
30–40 minutes
, for a fare of around
Jeepneys heading down from Maligcong to Bontoc cluster in the early morning and afternoon. If you miss one, you'll need to charter a tricycle or van, at around
one way.
From Sagada to Bontoc is about
1 hour
by jeepney or van, and from Banaue to Bontoc is about
2–3 hours
. From Bontoc, transfer to a Maligcong-bound jeepney.
If you're also stopping in Sagada, register in advance through the
Sagada iPass online registration
run by the municipality of Sagada and get a QR pass. Maligcong belongs to Bontoc, so a village environmental registration fee is paid separately from this registration.
The nearest international airport is Clark International Airport (CRK), about
9–11 hours
away via Baguio or Banaue. In practice, this trip is a bus journey from start to finish.
Maligcong's paddies generally yield one rice crop a year. Before planting, in
January–March
, the flooded paddies mirror the sky; planting follows in
March–April
, and by
May–July
the whole terrace turns deep green. Around
August

, the rice ripens to gold and harvest begins. The farming calendar varies a bit from year to year and village to village, so it's worth asking your homestay about the paddies' current state before you visit.
A sea of clouds is most likely on a cold, clear morning in
November–February
. Dawn temperatures during this period drop to around
, making the mountaintop quite cold.
June–October

is the rainy and typhoon season, with frequent rain, slippery mountain trails, and occasional landslides blocking Halsema Highway or the road toward Bontoc. If you're visiting during the rainy season, build extra time into your schedule.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
Maligcong has no hotels, only a handful of homestays run out of villagers' own homes. A shared room runs about
per person, and a private room runs about

; most homestays have you order meals separately. Some places have no hot water or charge extra for towels, so confirm when you book. Rooms fill up fast on peak-season weekends, so reserve ahead by social media or phone. To widen your options, you could also stay in Bontoc town (about
a night) and travel up by chartered vehicle before dawn.

Homestay meals center on simple home cooking — rice grown locally, stir-fried vegetables, eggs, and chicken. If it's available, be sure to try etag, smoked pork from the Cordillera highlands, or mountain-grown coffee. The village has almost no shops or restaurants, so it's best to buy snacks, water, and other essentials at the market in Bontoc town beforehand.
There's no ATM in Maligcong. Withdraw plenty of cash in Manila, Baguio, or Bontoc first.
Since the Kupapey sunrise hike starts in the dark before dawn, going with a local guide is standard practice. Ask your homestay to arrange one.
Bring a headlamp, hiking shoes with good grip, and a windbreaker. The mountaintop is chilly before dawn even in high summer.
Phone signal is weak and drops easily. Let family know your itinerary in advance and download an offline map.
Night falls early in the village. Avoid loud noise or drinking late at night.
The paddy walls are both villagers' workplace and private property. Stick to the path your guide shows you, and don't step into the paddies or block the water channels.
Ask permission before photographing residents or elders.
Jeepney schedules change frequently. On your day of departure, plan around a morning trip leaving around
, and confirm with your homestay the day before.
The stone paddy walls are narrow, and some drop several meters. They're very slippery with moss after rain, so walk slowly, and children or anyone afraid of heights shouldn't push themselves.
During the rainy season, landslides can cut off the road toward Bontoc. Check the weather and road conditions before you set out.
The environmental registration and guide fees can change under village rules. Check the latest notice and get a receipt.
Carry out all your trash, and use as few plastic bottles as possible.
On days with a village ritual or communal holiday (te-er), outsider access may be restricted, so follow local guidance.
It's easy to lose your way during the pre-dawn hike. Don't head into the dark forest trail without a guide.
